text: I used to think I could write and keep my phone face-up next to my laptop, but a single all-nighter last semester convinced me otherwise. I was drafting a fifteen-page paper on water policy, and every time a group chat lit up I told myself I would only glance for a second. Those seconds added up, and by 3 a.m. I had checked the screen maybe forty times and finished barely two pages. Each interruption, however brief, imposes a switching cost on the brain, and research indicates that it can take more than twenty minutes to fully restore one's attention to the original task after such a diversion. That number lined up uncomfortably well with my own experience that night. When I finally turned the phone off and shoved it in a drawer, the difference was almost embarrassing: I wrote more in the next ninety minutes than I had all evening. So while constant connectivity feels harmless and even productive, I am now convinced it quietly corrodes the kind of deep, sustained focus that real writing demands. The cost is not the minute you spend glancing down; it is the long climb back up afterward.
